docs.text: Learning from first principles, one point at a time. Each learning line is one main work plus its companions, and all lines link into one big picture.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
• Background: several years of CV research and PyTorch.
  • Goal: understand systems, CV and LLMs from first principles (be able to predict, explain and rebuild), not just use them.
  • Machines: Windows + WSL, and a remote Linux server (VS Code SSH). Labs run on the server.
  • Time: 60–90 min every day, first thing. 20-minute minimum on bad days. 30-minute review every week.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
docs/index.md                       ← this page: all lines, flow, rules
docs/<line>/index.md                ← a line's roadmap (sources, plan, Now, log)
docs/<line>/chNN/index.md           ← a unit's point map

docs/papers/<year>-<name>.md        ← one paper, e.g. papers/2012-alexnet.md

Starting a line: create docs/<line>/index.md from template A, add a row to the table above, and add it to nav in mkdocs.yml.

docs.title: How each point works
docs.text:
The same for every line:

  1. Questions first: answer without reading anything.
  2. If stuck: read the exact section of the source, then re-answer.
  3. Predict, then run: write down the expected output, then run the code test. Code + prediction + output go to Claude to check.
  4. Summary: in my own words, checked by Claude.
  5. Big picture: 2–4 links to other fields, one hop only, each with a check question answerable in about 5 minutes. Deeper links go on a "later" list. Each link is marked code or analogy.
  6. Mistakes log: what I got wrong, and why.

Status of each point: seen → can answer → can apply.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• At most 2–3 active lines at once.
  • Every answer and example is checked by running code.
  • Hints only for official course labs, never solutions. Solutions stay in a private repo.
  • Point IDs start with the line, e.g. csapp-2-01.
  • 80% learning, at most 20% writing pages.

docs.title: How a session ends
docs.text: Update the line's "Now" and log, then the "Now" section above. Commit.

docs.title: Site
docs.text:

docs.title: How pages work
docs.text:
Books and courses are learning lines: one main work plus its companions, e.g. a book and the course that follows it (CSAPP + CMU 15-213). Each line has a roadmap and one flat folder under docs/.

Papers are single pages in docs/papers/, named <year>-<short-name>.md (e.g. 2012-alexnet.md), whatever their field. A paper is short and self-contained, so it gets no roadmap and no folder. If a paper ever grows into a months-long study, turn it into its own line.

Categories (systems, CV, LLMs, ...) are tags, not folders; see Tags.

There are four kinds of page: a line roadmap (one per line), a unit point map (one per unit), a point (many per unit) and a paper page (one per paper).

docs/<line>/index.md                ← line roadmap
docs/<line>/chNN/index.md           ← unit point map
docs/<line>/chNN/<id>-<name>.md     ← points
docs/papers/index.md                ← table of papers + reading orders
docs/papers/<year>-<name>.md        ← one paper

Units follow the main source's structure: chapters for a book (ch02/), sections for a paper, lectures or modules for a course. Example: docs/csapp/index.md, docs/csapp/ch02/index.md and docs/csapp/ch02/csapp-2-01-hex.md.

Starting a new line: create its folder and index.md from template A, add a row to the home page table, and add it to nav in mkdocs.yml. Create a unit folder only when you reach that unit.

docs.title: How deep do big-picture links go?
docs.text:
One hop, at the level of the shared principle. A link shows that the same idea appears in another field. It doesn't teach that field.

  • 2–4 links per point, only where the link is real.
  • One hop only: link from this point to another field, never from that field on to a third.
  • Each link gets one check question I can answer in about 5 minutes from this point plus what I already know. If answering it needs a concept I haven't learned, the link is too deep.
  • Too deep? Don't follow it now. Write it in a "later" list. It can become its own point when that line is active.
  • Mark each link code (I checked it by running something) or analogy (understood, not verified).

docs.title: CSAPP: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
docs.text: Why I'm learning this: to understand what actually happens under the code I write in Python and PyTorch: data representation, machine code, memory, processes. Then I can predict performance and bugs instead of guessing.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
• Book: 3rd edition, Global Edition. Read the chapter text from it, but skip its practice and homework problems: the authors say that edition's problem set has many errors. Questions on this site are written separately and checked by running code. Sections are referenced by number (e.g. §2.1.3), not by page.
  • Book site (errata, self-study lab handouts): https://csapp.cs.cmu.edu/3e/
  • Companion source: CMU 15-213 (Introduction to Computer Systems, the course built on this book): slides, lectures and schedule, as a second explanation. The plan follows its order. https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~213/
  • Machine for labs: the remote Linux server (x86-64).
  • Lab solutions go in a private repo, not here.

docs.title: Ch2: Representing and manipulating information
docs.text:
The story of the chapter: everything is bits, and meaning comes from how the bits are read (§2.1). Integers have two encodings, unsigned and two's complement (§2.2). Fixed width makes integer arithmetic wrap around (§2.3). Floating point trades exactness for range (§2.4).

Lab: datalab. Integer puzzles after 2-11, float puzzles after 2-15.

Start here: take the placement quiz to mark the points I already know.

docs.title: Hex is shorthand for bits; data sizes come from the ABI, not from C
1. Questions
docs.text:
Answer first, without reading. No calculator for 1–5. Write your answers here, then send them to Claude to check.

  1. Write 0x39A7F8 in binary.

  2. Write 1100 1001 0111 1011 in hex.

  3. Write 2²³ in hex. What is 0x2000 in decimal?

  4. Work these out in hex: 167 (decimal → hex), 0x503C + 0x8, 0x503C − 0x40.

  5. A machine has 64-bit virtual addresses. How many bytes can it address? What is the highest address in hex? How many hex digits does a 64-bit value take?

  6. Fill in sizeof (in bytes) for Linux x86-64 and Windows x64: char, short, int, long, long long, void *, float, double, size_t.

  7. What does printf("%ld\n", (long)3000000000LL); print on each platform?

  8. Your PyTorch model has 1 billion parameters. How many bytes does it take in fp32, fp16/bf16 and int8? Is 2 GB more or less than 2 GiB? Why do some CUDA kernels break when a tensor has more than 0x7FFFFFFF elements?

docs.title: 2. If stuck, read
docs.text: • CSAPP §2.1.1 (hex notation, including the 2ⁿ trick) and §2.1.2 (data sizes, Figure 2.3). Then re-answer the questions above.

docs.title: 3. Predict, then run
docs.text:
Run this on Linux (WSL or the server): gcc -Wall -o sizes sizes.c && ./sizes. Write down your prediction for each line first. If you also have a Windows compiler, run it there too and compare.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>
int main(void) {
    printf("char %u short %u int %u long %u llong %u ptr %u size_t %u\n",
           (unsigned)sizeof(char), (unsigned)sizeof(short), (unsigned)sizeof(int),
           (unsigned)sizeof(long), (unsigned)sizeof(long long),
           (unsigned)sizeof(void *), (unsigned)sizeof(size_t));
    printf("%ld\n", (long)3000000000LL);
    printf("%#x %#x %#x\n", 0x503C + 0x8, 0x503C - 0x40, 1 << 23);
    return 0;
}

My prediction: ...

Actual output: ... Prediction right? yes / no, and why

docs.title: 5. Big picture
docs.text:
Shared principle: a number's width is fixed by a contract outside the language (the ABI, a file format, a dtype), and code that assumes a different width breaks silently.

Field Same principle there Check question Verified? ML dtypes Model memory = parameter count × dtype width What's the size of a 7B model in bf16, in GiB? CUDA / PyTorch int32 vs int64 index width limits tensor size Why does torch.int32 overflow at numel() > 2**31 - 1? Networking IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, IPv6 addresses are 128 bits written in hex groups How many hex digits are in a full IPv6 address?

docs.title: Ch2 placement quiz
docs.text:
One quick question per point, csapp-2-02 to csapp-2-15, to find what I already know. Assume C on x86-64 Linux, 32-bit int and two's complement.

How to use it: answer every question in one sitting (about 30 min), without reading the book or running code. Then send all answers to Claude, who checks them by running code.

  • Right, and I can say why: mark the point can answer in the point map. Skim its sections and do only its code test.
  • Wrong or guessed: do the full point flow.
Point Question 2-02 int x = 0x01234567 is stored at address 0x100 on a little-endian machine. Which byte is at 0x100, 0x101, 0x102 and 0x103? 2-03 unsigned x = 0xA1B2C3D4. What are x ^ ~0xFF and x \| 0xFF? Which one keeps the low byte and flips everything else? 2-04 int x = 0x5A, y = 0x0F. What are x & y, x && y, ~x \| ~y and !x \|\| !y? Then: int s = 0xF0000000 (as a bit pattern). What are s >> 4 and 0xF0000000u >> 4? 2-05 What's the unsigned value of the 8-bit pattern 1011 0110? 2-06 What's the same pattern's two's-complement value? Why is -INT_MIN == INT_MIN? 2-07 What are -1 < 0U and 2147483647U > -2147483647 - 1? What's wrong with for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)? 2-08 short sx = -12345; (0xCFC7). What's the hex of (int)sx, (int)(unsigned short)sx and (unsigned)sx? What's (short)53191? 2-09 In 8 bits: what's 100 + 100 signed, and 200 + 100 unsigned? How do you detect unsigned overflow of s = x + y using only s, x and y? 2-10 In 8 bits: what's -(-128) signed, 0xFF * 0xFF unsigned, and -3 * 50 signed? 2-11 Write x * 14 with two shifts and one subtraction. What are -7 / 4 and -7 >> 2? Make the shift version round toward zero. 2-12 Write 5.875 in binary. What's its 32-bit float bit pattern in hex? 2-13 Which float values do the bit patterns 0x00000001, 0x7F7FFFFF, 0x7F800000 and 0x7FC00000 encode? 2-14 Round 2.5, 3.5 and −2.5 to an integer using IEEE round-to-even. What's (int)(float)16777217? 2-15 In double, what are (1e16 + 1) - 1e16 and (1e16 - 1e16) + 1? Is 0.1f == 0.1 true?

docs.title: AlexNet (2012)
docs.text: Paper: Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton. ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2012.

docs.title: Reproduction notes
docs.text:
Originally written 2026-03-18 as "Reproducing AlexNet in 2026: The Spark of the Deep Learning Revolution" on PapersAI.

AlexNet (2012) is the "Big Bang" of modern AI. Before this paper, computer vision relied on hand-crafted features. After this paper, the world moved to end-to-end learning.

In this first project for PapersAI (PAI), I am reproducing the modernized AlexNet architecture using two major frameworks: PyTorch and JAX/Flax.

docs.title: 1. The Challenge: Bridging 2012 and 2026
docs.text:
The original paper was written for a world where GPUs had 3GB of memory. Today, I am reproducing this on an AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS using CPU-optimized XLA compilation.

To maintain feasibility, I am targeting the CIFAR-10 dataset (\(32 \times 32\) images), which requires a "Gentle AlexNet" modification—shrinking the massive \(11 \times 11\) kernels to a more appropriate \(3 \times 3\) size.

docs.title: The PyTorch Approach (Object-Oriented)
docs.text: My PyTorch implementation follows the standard nn.Module pattern, leveraging nn.Sequential for the feature extractor. I chose to follow the torchvision variant, focusing on stability and modularity.

docs.title: The JAX/Flax Approach (Functional)
docs.text:
In JAX, state management is explicit. I used the Flax Linen library to define a @nn.compact model. This version is particularly interesting because it utilizes the XLA (Accelerated Linear Algebra) compiler to squeeze high performance out of my AMD Ryzen CPU.

Key Discovery: While PyTorch uses Channels-First (NCHW) by default, JAX prefers Channels-Last (NHWC). Handling this transition was a crucial part of ensuring framework parity.

docs.title: 3. Implementation Details
docs.text:
The model consists of 5 Convolutional layers and 3 Fully Connected layers.

Feature Original (2012) My Reproduction (PAI) Input Size \(224 \times 224\) \(32 \times 32\) (CIFAR-10) Normalization LRN Modern (None/BatchNorm) Optimizer SGD + Momentum SGD + StepLR Hardware 2x GTX 580 GPUs AMD Ryzen 7 CPU (XLA)

docs.title: 4. Visualizing the "Internal Brain"
docs.text:
(Once I finish training, I will upload the kernel visualizations here!)

Below is the LRN formula that gave AlexNet its edge in 2012, which I have implemented manually in the JAX version:

\[ b^i_{x,y} = \frac{a^i_{x,y}}{\left(k + \alpha \sum_{j} (a^j_{x,y})^2\right)^\beta} \]
